title: Describing precisely
cando: describe people, places and things in detail

about.text: In this lesson you describe people, places and things in detail, so that nobody needs to ask again. You compare two quotes for the same job, and you read a catalogue entry and a returns form. Then you describe a lost bag so precisely that the lost property office finds it first time.
goals: Say which one you mean with who, which, that, where and whose.
Put adjectives in the right order: a small brown leather bag.
Use two-word adjectives: a well-made chair, a ten-minute walk.
Read a catalogue entry and a returns form, and describe a lost item.
Describe a lost item so precisely that someone can find it.

chapters.title: Two quotes, one job
chapters.text:
This lesson is about describing things precisely, so that nobody needs to ask again.
First, you listen to Nadia and Diego. They run a small café, and they need a new counter. Two firms have sent them quotes. One is cheap, and one is more expensive.
Listen for three useful phrases. It's the one that… It's a kind of… What does it look like?
Listen for the price, the material and the size of each counter. Then decide: which one is better value for money?

chapters.title: Which one, and what is it like?
chapters.text:
Now, the grammar. To say which one you mean, use who, which, that, where and whose.
Who is for people: the woman who found my wallet. Which is for things: the bag which I lost. That is for people or things: the firm that made our counter.
Where is for places: the café where we met. And whose is for belonging: the man whose bag was stolen.
Then, adjective order. First your opinion, then size, age, shape, colour and material, and last the noun. A lovely small brown leather bag.
Two words can also make one adjective: a well-made chair, a hand-made table, a ten-minute walk. With a number, the noun stays singular. Say a ten-minute walk, not a ten-minutes walk.

chapters.title: A catalogue and a returns form
chapters.text:
Next, you read a page from a shop's catalogue. It describes a leather bag and a purse: the size, the weight, the colour, and what's inside. Read the numbers carefully.
Then you read a returns form. A customer's new bag arrived with a broken zip and a long scratch. Notice how specific she is. She doesn't just say it's bad. She says what is wrong, and where.
After that, you write a description of something you have lost, for a lost property office.

chapters.title: At the lost property office
chapters.text:
Then you go to the lost property office at a station. You left your bag on a train, and the office has three bags that look almost the same.
Describe yours so precisely that they find it first time. Say the size, the colour and the material. Say what's inside. And give one detail that only the owner knows. For example: There's a small scratch on the front, near the zip.
Give facts, not opinions. Don't say: It's a nice bag. Say: It's a dark green leather bag with a long strap.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text: Last, you read a longer story or article. Notice how the writer describes people and places, and which small details make them easy to picture. Read it once for the story, then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: You need a builder for a job at home. How do you choose one?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people ask two or three firms for a quote and compare them carefully. To compare well, you need to describe things precisely.

conversation.title: Two quotes for a new counter
conversation.setting: Nadia and Diego run a small café. They need a new counter, and two firms have sent them quotes. They look at the quotes together before the café opens.
lines: The two quotes for the new counter have arrived. Shall we have a look?
Yes. Remind me, which firm is Linden's?
It's the one that made the counter in the bakery on King Street.
Oh, the bakery where we had lunch last week? I loved that counter.
That's the one. Their quote is £3,200, which is reasonable for a hand-made counter in solid oak.
Fitwell Direct. Their quote is only £2,100, but the counter is made of chipboard.
It's a kind of board that's made from small pieces of wood and glue. It's cheaper, but it isn't as strong.
I see. And what does the oak one look like?
It's pale, with a smooth surface, and the front has a striped pattern. It's approximately two metres wide and it weighs about ninety kilos.
Ninety kilos! Well, our back wall is solid brick, so that should be fine.
So, which one is better value for money?
Linden's, I think. It's more expensive, but it will last. Let's ask them for a specific start date.

questions.q: How does Nadia know Linden's work?
questions.a: She saw their counter in a bakery.
wrong: They made the counter in her café.
Diego used to work for them.
questions.why: Linden's made the counter in the bakery where Nadia had lunch last week.

questions.a: a board made from small pieces of wood and glue
questions.why: Diego says: It's a kind of board that's made from small pieces of wood and glue.
Nadia says: It's more expensive, but it will last.

phrases.text: It's the one that made the counter in the bakery.

phrases.use: Explaining something that the other person doesn't know.

phrases.text: It's pale, with a smooth surface.
phrases.use: Describing the colour and the surface.
Giving a size that is not exact.

phrases.text: Which one is better value for money?
phrases.use: Comparing the price and the quality.

items.meaning: A written price that a business gives you for a job before the work starts.
items.example: We asked three builders for a quote for the new roof.

items.meaning: A business or a company, usually a small or medium-sized one.
items.example: She works for a small firm of accountants in the city centre.

items.meaning: Fair and sensible. A price like this is not too high.
items.example: The rent is reasonable for a flat so close to the station.

items.meaning: Worth the price you pay, because the quality is good.
items.example: The cheap sofa wasn't good value for money: it broke after a year.

items.meaning: Exact and clear, with all the details.
items.example: Can you give me a specific date for the delivery?

items.meaning: About, but not exactly.
items.example: The journey takes approximately forty minutes.

items.meaning: How wide something is, from one side to the other.
items.example: Measure the width of the door before you buy the fridge.

items.meaning: Very, very big.
items.example: They've built an enormous supermarket outside the town.

items.meaning: Light in colour, with not much colour in it.
items.example: We painted the office walls pale green.

items.meaning: With lines of different colours on it.
items.example: He was wearing a blue and white striped shirt.

items.meaning: Shapes or lines that repeat on cloth, paper or another surface.
items.example: I like the curtains, but not the flower pattern.

items.meaning: The top or the outside part of something.
items.example: Clean the surface of the table with a dry cloth.

items.meaning: Hard and strong, or made of one material all the way through.
items.example: The table is solid wood, so it's very heavy.

items.meaning: A hard block of baked clay. Builders use it to make walls and houses.
items.example: Our house is built of red brick.

items.meaning: To have a certain heaviness, or to measure how heavy something is.
items.example: My suitcase weighs twenty-three kilos.

sound.title: Stress in long describing words
sound.explain: Long words have one strong part. In reasonable, valuable and catalogue, the stress is on the first part: REA-son-a-ble. In enormous, specific and approximately, it is on the second part: e-NOR-mous. Listen, then say each group. Make the strong part longer and louder.

sayIt.instructions: Say Diego's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Is the stress clear in the long words?
lines: It's the one that made the counter in the bakery on King Street.
It's a kind of board that's made from small pieces of wood and glue.
It's pale, with a smooth surface, and the front has a striped pattern.
It's approximately two metres wide and it weighs about ninety kilos.

spot.instructions: Look at these words from the conversation. Each one gives more information about a thing or a place.
examples: It's the one that made the counter in the bakery on King Street.
Oh, the bakery where we had lunch last week?
Their quote is £3,200, which is reasonable.
a hand-made counter in solid oak
spot.question: Which word adds information about the firm? Which one is about a place? Which one comes after a comma? And which two words work together as one adjective?
spot.answer: that adds information about the firm: the one that made the counter. where is for a place: the bakery where we had lunch. which comes after a comma and adds extra information about the quote. hand-made is two words with a hyphen, and they work as one adjective.

rules.title: who, which, that, where, whose
rule: People: who or that. The woman who found my wallet.
Things: which or that. The bag which I lost. The firm that made our counter.
Places: where. The café where we met. Belonging: whose. The man whose bag was stolen.
Extra information goes between commas, with who or which, never that: The quote, which was £3,200, was reasonable.
You can leave out who, which or that when it is not the subject: the bag I lost.
rules.mistake: Not: the man which lives next door. Say: the man who lives next door.

rules.title: Adjective order and two-word adjectives
rule: Order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, material, then the noun.
a lovely old oval mirror; a small black leather bag
Two words with a hyphen can make one adjective: a well-made chair, a hand-made table.
With a number, the noun stays singular: a ten-minute walk, not a ten-minutes walk.
rules.mistake: Not: a leather black small bag. Say: a small black leather bag.

practice.q: The counter ___ they made for us is solid oak.
practice.why: that or which for a thing: the counter that they made.

practice.q: That's the café ___ we had lunch last week.
practice.why: where for a place: the café where we had lunch.

practice.q: The man ___ bag was lost on the train has called again.
practice.why: whose for belonging: his bag, so whose bag.

practice.q: The woman ___ found my wallet didn't leave her name.
The office is a ___ walk from the station.
practice.why: With a number, the noun stays singular: a ten-minute walk.

practice.q: It's a well-___ chair. It will last for years.
practice.why: well + made makes one adjective: a well-made chair.

practice.q: My neighbour, ___ is a builder, gave us a quote.
practice.why: Extra information about a person, between commas: who, never that.
Extra information about a thing, between commas: which, never that.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of three things you own: something you wear, something you carry and something in your home. Describe each one in one or two sentences. Put the adjectives in the right order, and use who, which, that, where or whose.
yourTurn.model: My favourite coat is a long dark blue woollen coat that I bought in Edinburgh. I always carry a small brown leather bag which my sister gave me. In my living room there's an old oval mirror whose frame is painted gold. It's a kind of mirror that you often see in old hotels.

text.title: A catalogue entry and a returns form
text.body:
PRACTICE PAGE: this shop does not exist.
HARTLEY & STONE · AUTUMN CATALOGUE · PAGE 14
ITEM 2041 · THE CAMDEN WORK BAG · £89
A well-made, medium-sized bag in soft brown leather, hand-stitched in our own workshop.
Size: width 38 cm, height 29 cm, depth 10 cm. Weight: approximately 900 g.
Outside: a front pocket with a brass zip, and a long strap.
Inside: space for a 15-inch laptop, and a zipped pocket for your valuable belongings.
Every bag has a small numbered tag inside, so you can identify it if it is lost.
Care: clean the surface with a dry cloth. Leather shows small marks and scratches over time. This is normal.
ITEM 2042 · THE CAMDEN PURSE · £35
A small oval purse in the same leather, with a striped cotton lining. Holds cards, coins and notes.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE FORM: this shop does not exist.
HARTLEY & STONE · RETURNS FORM
Order number: HS-55812   Name: Priya Nair
Item: The Camden Work Bag, brown (item 2041)
Reason for return (tick one):
[ ] Changed my mind   [x] Damaged or faulty   [ ] Not as described   [ ] Wrong item
Describe the problem. Please be specific: we cannot help if you only write 'it's bad'.
The zip on the front pocket is broken, and there is a long scratch on the back of the bag. The box was in perfect condition, so the damage probably happened before it was packed.
What would you like us to do?
[x] Send me a new one   [ ] Give me my money back
Returns are free within 30 days. Please send back all the contents of the box: the bag, the strap and the dust bag.

gist.q: What does the catalogue page do?
gist.a: It describes two leather items for sale.
wrong: It explains how to return an item.
It lists things found on a train.
gist.why: It gives the size, the colour and the price of a bag and a purse.

gist.q: Why did Priya fill in the returns form?
wrong: She changed her mind about the colour.
The shop sent her the purse, not the bag.
gist.why: She ticked Damaged or faulty: the zip is broken and there is a scratch.

detail.q: How much does the work bag weigh?
detail.why: The catalogue says: Weight: approximately 900 g.
The catalogue says: A small oval purse.

detail.q: How can you identify a Camden bag if you lose it?
wrong: by the colour of the zip
by the name on the strap
detail.why: Every bag has a small numbered tag inside, so you can identify it.

detail.q: Why does Priya think the bag was damaged before it was packed?
detail.a: The box was in perfect condition.
detail.why: She writes: The box was in perfect condition, so the damage probably happened before it was packed.

items.meaning: Things that people have lost or left behind, or the office that keeps them.
items.example: I asked at lost property, and they had my umbrella.

items.meaning: A list or a book of things for sale, with pictures and details.
items.example: I ordered the lamp from their online catalogue.

items.meaning: One thing on a list, or one thing in a group.
items.example: Each item on the list has a number.

items.meaning: How good or bad something is: new, old, broken and so on.
items.example: The bike is ten years old, but it's in excellent condition.

items.meaning: The things that are inside something, like a bag or a box.
items.example: Please describe the contents of your bag.

items.meaning: The things that you own and carry with you.
items.example: Please take all your belongings with you when you leave the train.

items.meaning: Worth a lot of money, or very useful.
items.example: Don't leave anything valuable in your car.

items.meaning: Material made from the skin of an animal. It is used for shoes, bags and jackets.
items.example: It's a brown leather wallet with my initials on it.

items.meaning: A thin line on a surface, made by something sharp.
items.example: There's a small scratch on the screen of my phone.

items.meaning: Shaped like an egg.
items.example: We bought an oval table for the kitchen.

items.meaning: To say or show who someone is, or what something is.
items.example: Can you identify your bag? What's inside it?

model.title: A lost item: my laptop bag
model.body:
Lost item: a laptop bag
Where and when: on the number 42 bus from the city centre, on Tuesday 14 October, at about 6.30 pm
Description: It's a medium-sized black leather bag with a long strap. It's approximately 40 cm wide. There's a scratch on the front, near the zip, and one end of the strap is fixed with black tape.
Contents: a silver laptop, a blue notebook and a pair of glasses in a brown case
How to identify it: The laptop is the one that has a red bicycle sticker on the cover. My name, Omar Khalil, is on a small card in the front pocket.
Phone: 07700 900 518

write.task: Imagine you have lost something valuable: a bag, a coat, a phone or a wallet. Write a description for the lost property office, like the model. Say where and when you lost it, what it looks like, what is inside it, and how they can identify it.
checklist: I said where and when I lost it.
I put two or three adjectives in the right order: a small black leather bag.
I used which, that or whose to add a detail.
I gave one detail that only the owner would know.

card.title: At the lost property office
card.situation: Yesterday evening, you left your bag on a train. Today you go to the lost property office at the station. The office has a lot of bags, and some of them look almost the same as yours.
card.goal: Describe your bag and what is inside it so precisely that the officer finds it first time. Give one detail that shows it is yours.

phrases: I left my bag on the 6.15 train from Leeds yesterday.
It's a medium-sized dark green leather bag.
It's the one that has a long striped strap.
Inside, there's a laptop whose cover has a red sticker.
There's a small scratch on the front, near the zip.
prepare.notes: Picture your bag. Make notes on its size, colour, material and shape, what is inside it, and one detail that only you would know.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher works at the lost property office and has three bags that look similar. Describe yours so the teacher can find it first time. Then change roles.
doIt.wehel: You work at the lost property office at a train station. I left my bag on a train yesterday. Imagine you have three bags that look similar. Ask me about my bag: its size, colour and material, what is inside it, and anything special about it. Only give me my bag when my description is precise. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Which bag is yours?
lines: Good morning. How can I help?
Hello. I left my bag on the train from Leeds yesterday evening. It was the 6.15.
It's a medium-sized dark green leather bag, with a long striped strap.
We've got three green bags. Is it the one with the brass zip?
No, mine has a black zip. And there's a small scratch on the front, near the zip.
A silver laptop, a blue notebook and a pair of glasses in a brown case.
Is there anything that shows it's yours?
Yes. My laptop has a red sticker on the cover, and there's a card with my name in the front pocket: Lena Novak.
Let me check… Yes, here it is. Can I see something with your name on it, please?
Of course. Here's my bank card. Thank you so much!
compare: Did you say where and when you lost it?
Did you give the size, the colour and the material in the right order?
Did you say what was inside?
Did you give one detail that only the owner would know?

canDo: I can describe people, places and things in detail.
I can say which one I mean with who, which, that, where and whose.
I can put two or three adjectives in the right order.
I can read a catalogue entry and a returns form.
I can describe a lost item so precisely that someone can find it.

reading.before: Look at the title and the pictures. Which person, place or thing do you think the writer will describe most carefully?
reading.talk: Choose one person, place or thing from the book. Describe it in three or four sentences, with as much detail as you can. Or describe it to Wehel, and ask Wehel to guess what it is.

quiz.q: That's the woman ___ found my wallet.
Is this the station ___ you lost your bag?
The customer ___ phone was stolen is at the desk.
quiz.why: whose for belonging: her phone, so whose phone.

quiz.q: It's a ___ walk to the office.
quiz.why: With a number, the noun stays singular: a five-minute walk.

quiz.q: A written price for a job, before the work starts, is a ___ .
quiz.why: A firm gives you a quote before the job starts.

quiz.q: The things that you own and carry with you are your ___ .
quiz.why: belongings = the things that you own and carry with you.
After did, write use to, with no d.

quiz.q: How long have you ___ living in this flat?
quiz.why: The present perfect continuous: have + been + -ing.
2019 is a finished time, so we use the past simple.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Nadia and Diego's conversation in pairs. Then play a guessing game: one learner describes something in the room with It's a kind of … and It's the one that …, and the others guess.

Day 2: bring three bags or coats to class. Learners describe each one with adjectives in the right order and a who, which or whose clause. Check two-word adjectives: a well-made coat, a ten-minute walk.
Day 3: the task. You work at the lost property office and have three similar bags. Each learner describes their lost bag until you can find it first time.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and let two learners read their lost-item descriptions aloud while the others draw the item.
